content: The acceptability of a diagnostic test for pyrazinamide resistance depends on its ability to accurately detect mutations associated with resistance. Clinicians and laboratory staff may need further clarification and justification for prioritizing this specific drug test, especially since it is not currently part of routine drug susceptibility testing (DST). The implementation of a pyrazinamide line probe assay (LPA) faces challenges due to the significant training and laboratory infrastructure required. Additionally, the availability of an automated interpretation system is crucial, as the results can be difficult to interpret. When implementing a high-complexity hybridization-based nucleic acid amplification test (NAAT) for pyrazinamide resistance detection, several factors must be considered. These include the complexity of the test, the difficulty in interpreting results due to the large number of bands, and the need for local epidemiological data to guide testing algorithms. Pretest probability is also important for clinical interpretation. The cost of the test varies depending on factors such as batch size, staff time, and other parameters, necessitating a local cost analysis. Tests with varying levels of complexity require increasing technical competency, staff time, and resources, which impact planning and budgeting. Local support services and maintenance timelines should also be considered when selecting a provider. Laboratory accreditation and compliance with a robust quality management system, including appropriate quality control, are essential for sustained service excellence. Recommendations include the use of connectivity solutions to improve the efficiency of result communication and reduce the time to treatment initiation. Pyrazinamide resistance is significantly associated with rifampicin resistance in all settings. Implementing high-complexity hybridization-based NAATs requires laboratories with adequate infrastructure, space, and functional sample referral systems. The manual steps involved in these assays necessitate well-trained staff for setup and instrument maintenance. Special training and experience are required to interpret banding patterns on the test strips. The impact of specific mutations on treatment outcomes among patients with drug-resistant tuberculosis (DR-TB) should be further studied. Additionally, the integration and optimization of diagnostic technologies within the broader landscape of testing and care, as well as their economic implications, need to be evaluated. Qualitative studies assessing equity, acceptability, feasibility, and end-user values of diagnostic technologies are also important. The interpretation of results from high-complexity hybridization-based NAATs should be compared with sequencing and newer evidence on genotypic and phenotypic associations. The World Health Organization (WHO) guidelines on tuberculosis diagnostics emphasize the importance of systematic reviews to assess the performance and use of diagnostic tools. The certainty of evidence is evaluated using the GRADE approach, which provides a framework for translating evidence into recommendations. Factors influencing the direction and strength of recommendations include the priority of the problem, test accuracy, balance of benefits and harms, certainty of evidence, resource requirements, cost-effectiveness, equity, acceptability, and feasibility. The feasibility of implementing a diagnostic tool depends on factors such as training needs, biosafety requirements, time to results, service and maintenance, and its impact on diagnostic algorithms. Acceptability is assessed based on the perspectives of stakeholders, including healthcare workers, managers, and patients. Resource requirements, including costs and cost-effectiveness, are also evaluated.
